strengths: The paper addresses a real and clearly-articulated gap: existing audio captioning/QA benchmarks reward generic captions and rely on close-ended QA formats. The motivating analysis (e.g., the Wrong/Safe/Right case study in Figure 5) convincingly demonstrates that BLEU-1 and FENSE fail to separate detailed from vague outputs.

MECAT is a substantial contribution: ~20k clips from a novel source (ACAV100M), eight domains including mixed-domain scenes, 18 reference captions per clip, and >100k open-ended QA pairs organized into a sensible cognitive taxonomy (Perception/Analysis/Reasoning). The vocabulary-size comparison (Appendix A) supports the claimed lexical richness.

The multi-expert annotation pipeline (specialized speech/music/sound/quality models + CoT LLM synthesis + rule-based and embedding-based filtering) is well documented, with complete model lists (Appendix B), full prompts (Appendix C), and judge prompts (Appendix D), which aids reproducibility.

The DATE metric is a reasonable, computationally cheap design: tf-idf-weighted Sentence-BERT similarity plus cross-sample discriminability. The CDF analysis (Figure 6) shows larger Right-vs-Wrong and Right-vs-Safe separations than FENSE, approaching LLM-as-judge behavior at much lower cost.

The model evaluation yields genuinely informative findings: limited capability on content-unrelated (acoustic property) tasks across all models, degradation on mixed vs. pure domains, sub-category specializations (e.g., Kimi-Audio's weakness on Quality Assessment), and a small 3B-vs-7B gap suggesting architectural/training factors matter more than scale.

The authors validate LLM-as-judge as a reference metric with Fleiss' Kappa analysis (Appendix E) and are upfront that it has only moderate reliability for captioning (κ=0.43), using it as an upper-bound reference rather than ground truth.
weaknesses: No human validation of the benchmark annotations. The central premise is that machine-generated fine-grained captions are more informative than human ones, yet annotation accuracy is never audited by human listeners. Given known hallucination rates in the constituent expert models (emotion, accent, age recognition, LALM descriptions, DeepSeek-R1 synthesis), even a small human audit of a few hundred captions/QA pairs would be expected. The quality-control stage (GLAP similarity filtering with an unclearly specified 'threshold of 6') does not establish factual correctness.
Potential model-circularity: Audio Flamingo 2 is a key component of the annotation pipeline and is also one of the evaluated models, which could bias its score favorably. This is not discussed.

DATE's validation is indirect: it is only compared against LLM-as-judge (itself only moderately reliable for captioning) on synthetic Right/Safe/Wrong response sets. There is no correlation study with human judgments, which is the standard evidence expected for a proposed evaluation metric.

The cross-sample discriminability term depends on the composition of the full candidate set and reference set (rank over N samples), making DATE scores dataset-dependent and sensitive to distractor selection; this property, and how three synonymous references per sample are combined in the similarity matrix, is under-specified.

Several details impair reproducibility: the code/data link in the abstract is empty ('avaiable at' with no URL); the QC threshold, the '6 other randomly selected captions', scoring weights (0.4/0.4/0.2, 0.8/0.2, 0.6/0.3/0.1), and difficulty distribution are empirically set but not justified or ablated.

Presentation sloppiness undermines confidence: the FENSE citation is wrong (cited as a software-engineering defect-prediction paper rather than the audio captioning metric by Zhou et al. 2022), typos throughout ('stands iI sharp contrast', 'provide' vs 'provides', 'avaiable'), and a duplicate numbering of Appendices E and F.

Open-ended QA answers are scored via a metric designed for captions (embedding similarity to a single reference answer); how DATE handles short/long/paraphrased answers and why it is appropriate for QA is not analyzed separately beyond the aggregate CDF plot.

Some evaluation choices are limited: only six models evaluated, no significance testing or variance reporting, and the silence domain has only 179 samples, making claims about extended multi-domain coverage thin at the extremes.

strengths: The benchmark addresses a real and well-motivated problem: existing audio captioning/QA benchmarks reward generic captions and closed-ended formats, and MECAT's extended multi-domain design (pure and mixed domains including silence) plus taxonomy of QA cognitive skills (Perception/Analysis/Reasoning) is a sensible structure for probing fine-grained understanding.

The dataset is relatively large (20k clips, 100k+ QA pairs) with 18 reference captions per clip, and Appendix A's vocabulary comparison (22,595 vs. 1.2k-5.6k for prior sets) supports the claim of richer annotations.

The DATE metric idea — combining tf-idf-weighted semantic similarity with a cross-sample discriminability (retrieval-style ranking) term — is a reasonable, lightweight approach to penalizing generic captions, and the CDF analysis (Figure 6) plus the Right/Safe/Wrong case study illustrate the intended discriminative behavior.

The appendices are unusually thorough: the full LLM synthesis prompt, expert model list, LLM-as-judge prompts and rubrics, and evaluation prompts are all provided, which aids transparency of the pipeline.

The model evaluation surfaces interpretable findings (e.g., the speech-focused Kimi-Audio failing on Quality Assessment, weak Content-Unrelated performance across all models) that suggest the benchmark can diagnose model biases.
weaknesses: The ground truth is entirely model-generated: expert models plus DeepSeek-R1 produce all captions and QA answers, and quality control consists only of model-based filtering (GLAP similarity, confidence thresholding, rule-based checks). There is no human verification or human evaluation of annotation accuracy anywhere in the paper. For a benchmark paper, unvalidated machine-generated references are a fundamental soundness concern — the benchmark may largely measure agreement with the annotation pipeline's biases (including Audio Flamingo 2, which is also one of the evaluated models, creating a potential conflict).

The DATE metric is not validated against human judgment. The only validation is against LLM-as-judge (used as an 'upper bound'), yet the paper's own Appendix E reports only moderate inter-rater reliability for captioning (κ = 0.43), and the 'Safe' condition is not even evaluated for QA (missing entry in the Appendix E table). 'Larger CDF separation' between constructed Right/Safe/Wrong sets is a weak proxy for metric quality.

The cross-sample discriminability term may penalize valid but atypical answers: ranking a candidate against all other references assumes references are mutually distinguishable, which is untested, and there is no analysis of DATE's behavior on open-ended QA answers with diverse valid paraphrases.

Key design choices are unjustified: the scoring weights (0.4/0.4/0.2, 0.8/0.2, 0.6/0.3/0.1 for Speech/Music/Sound) appear arbitrary, and the quality-control threshold is described only as an 'empirically set threshold of 6' with no units or sensitivity analysis.

Reproducibility is undermined: the abstract states 'The data and code are avaiable at' with no actual link, and no URL appears anywhere in the manuscript. Several cited works also appear miscited or undefined (the FENSE citation is a software-engineering defect-prediction paper, not the audio captioning metric; 'StrongDescriber' in Appendix A is never introduced in the text).

The evaluated model set is small (6 captioning models, 4 QA models) and omits several prominent LALMs (e.g., Qwen-Audio, SALMONN, GAMA), limiting the evidential strength of the capability claims and the generality of the '20-60% performance' conclusion.

No limitations section; privacy/ethics concerns (inference of age, gender, emotion, and accent of speakers from YouTube-sourced audio, and licensing of ACAV100M-derived content) are not discussed. Writing quality is also uneven (e.g., 'avaiable', 'a audio classification', 'provide' vs. 'provides'), suggesting insufficient polish.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and timely gap: existing audio captioning/QA benchmarks reward generic descriptions and closed-ended answer formats. The motivation is clearly articulated and well-supported by the related-work analysis.

MECAT is a substantial resource: ~20k clips from a novel source (ACAV100M subset, avoiding AudioSet/Clotho overlap), 18 reference captions per clip, over 100k QA pairs, and a well-motivated 'extended multi-domain' taxonomy (pure and mixed speech/music/sound/silence domains) that enables evaluation on complex acoustic scenes.

The annotation pipeline is thoughtfully designed and thoroughly documented: multiple specialized expert models (speech, music, sound events, acoustic properties), CoT-based LLM synthesis, and multi-stage quality control (embedding-based filtering, confidence thresholding, hallucination removal). Prompts and the full model list are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.

The DATE metric is a sensible, computationally cheap alternative to LLM-as-judge, combining tf-idf-weighted semantic similarity with cross-sample discriminability. The CDF analysis (Figure 6) and case studies demonstrate it discriminates between Right/Safe/Wrong responses better than FENSE.

The evaluation of six models yields concrete, actionable findings (e.g., performance gaps on reasoning vs. perception subtasks, weakness of all models on content-unrelated acoustic-property description, non-linear scaling with parameter count), demonstrating the benchmark's diagnostic value.
Appendices provide vocabulary-size comparison, LLM-as-judge validation with Fleiss' Kappa, and all evaluation/annotation prompts.
weaknesses: No human verification of the benchmark annotations. All captions and QA pairs are LLM-generated from other models' outputs, so errors propagate through the expert pipeline into the 'gold' labels. The quality-control stage is itself model- and rule-based. Since MECAT's central claim is that prior benchmarks are unreliable due to annotation quality, the absence of a human audit (e.g., expert review of a sample of captions for factual accuracy and hallucination rate) is a significant evidential gap.

Validation of DATE is indirect and somewhat circular. It is benchmarked against LLM-as-judge using synthetically constructed response tiers (Right/Safe/Wrong), where 'Wrong' responses are trivially incorrect (references from other samples). This setup likely inflates the apparent discriminability gap; correlation with actual human judgments of model outputs is not reported. Moreover, the LLM-as-judge reference itself only achieves moderate agreement for captioning (kappa = 0.43).

The cross-sample discriminability term may conflate factual detail with stylistic/lexical overlap with the reference set, potentially rewarding paraphrase-like outputs over equally accurate but differently phrased ones, and the tf-idf weighting depends on the benchmark's own corpus statistics. These risks are not analyzed.

The scoring aggregation weights (0.4/0.4/0.2, 0.8/0.2, 0.6/0.3/0.1) are unmotivated and arbitrary; sensitivity of the reported model rankings to these choices is not examined. The domain distribution is also highly skewed (7,839 speech-only vs. 179 silence), which is not discussed.

Some presentation issues undermine polish: the data/code URL is missing in the abstract (a reproducibility concern for a benchmark paper); typos ('avaiable', 'provide' vs 'provides', several in Appendix B); appendix cross-referencing is inconsistent (Table F.1/F.2 referenced as C.1/C.2); and Figure 5's 'Safe' vs. 'Right' example appears constructed rather than sampled from the evaluated models.

Evaluation breadth is limited on the QA side (only four LALMs, no caption-only baselines) and DATE is applied to open-set QA where semantic similarity scoring is a cruder fit than for captioning; no error analysis of DATE on QA is provided.

Limitations and ethics are addressed only briefly in the conclusion. Issues such as potential accent/language bias inherited from ACAV100M and expert models, licensing of the released annotations, and the safety of redistributing YouTube-derived audio deserve more explicit treatment.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: existing audio benchmarks reward generic captions, and the paper clearly articulates both the annotation-side and metric-side causes of this problem.

MECAT is substantial in scale and breadth: ~20k clips from a novel source (ACAV100M rather than the over-used AudioSet/Clotho pool), ~100k QA pairs, 18 reference captions per clip across six sub-categories, and an eight-domain taxonomy covering pure and mixed acoustic scenes.
The annotation pipeline is well-documented (expert models, LLM-CoT synthesis prompts, and QC stages are all provided in appendices), supporting reproducibility.

Validation is unusually thorough for an auto-constructed benchmark: a 150-pair human A/B preference test (94%+ win rates vs. safe/wrong captions, statistical parity with human references), an independent audit of 700 samples by 20 audio professionals with proper statistical testing (Wilcoxon, Bonferroni correction, effect sizes), and an honest reporting of the ~10% survival rate of the filtering pipeline.

The DATE metric is validated from multiple angles: qualitative case studies, CDF-based discriminability analysis, bootstrap stability analysis (CV < 1% at full scale), a sensitivity analysis of the heuristic ScoreCap weights (Kendall's tau = 0.92), and alignment with human preferences (mean 90.9 vs 49.3).

Evaluation of 17 captioning models and 15 QA models yields genuinely useful findings (speech-centric bias, degradation on mixed domains, weakness in quality-assessment/reasoning sub-tasks, hallucination on silence), with the transparency of flagging Audio Flamingo 3 whose predecessor was used in data construction.
The limitations section and impact statement are honest and substantive, acknowledging residual annotation noise, the 10-second scope, and DATE's inherited embedding limitations.
weaknesses: Circularity concerns are only partially addressed: annotations are generated by LALM/expert models, and evaluated LALMs are compared against LLM-generated references. The authors flag Audio Flamingo 3 but do not analyze contamination for models trained on corpora overlapping ACAV100M or expert-model outputs (e.g., WavCaps-style LLM-labeled data), nor do they report agreement between pipeline-generated references and independent human annotations at scale beyond the 700-sample audit.

The DATE metric is developed and validated primarily on MECAT itself; its discriminability component is dataset-relative, so a model could in principle optimize verbose, discriminative-sounding text without being more accurate. The N=150 human-preference validation is supportive but modest, and no validation on external datasets is provided.

Some pipeline details are under-specified or confusing, e.g., the GLAP filtering threshold ('exceeds ... by an empirically set threshold of 6' is unclear for a similarity quantity), and the basis for the QA answer generation (answers derived from expert model outputs may reflect expert-model biases rather than audio ground truth).

The A/B test instruction ('accuracy first, then level of detail') and DATE's design may conflate detail/verbosity with correctness; there is no ablation isolating whether DATE penalizes factually wrong but detailed captions.

Writing quality is uneven: an empty 'Conflict of Interest Disclosure' section, an incomplete GitHub URL in the abstract, and several typos (e.g., 'MECAT provide', 'Diariazation', 'Seperation', 'Recogintion') suggest insufficient proofreading.

Mixed-model evaluation introduces uncertainty in cross-model comparability (some evaluated models share lineage with pipeline components like DeepSeek-R1 synthesis or Sentence-BERT-era embeddings), which is not discussed.

strengths: Large-scale, openly released benchmark (~20k CC-licensed clips from ACAV100M, >100k QA pairs) that avoids AudioSet redundancy and covers eight mixed/pure audio domains, addressing a genuine gap in fine-grained audio evaluation.

Multi-perspective annotation taxonomy (systemic, content-specific, content-unrelated captions; six cognitive QA categories) is well designed and would enable more diagnostic evaluation than existing yes/no or multiple-choice benchmarks.

Substantial validation effort: human A/B preference test, a 20-professional audit of 700 samples with appropriate statistical testing (Wilson CIs, Wilcoxon with Bonferroni correction), weighting-sensitivity analysis (Kendall's tau = 0.92), and bootstrap stability analysis of DATE.

Honest limitations section acknowledging clip-length scope, residual annotation noise, and DATE's dependence on test-set diversity; impact statement addresses privacy risks of fine-grained captioning.
Extensive evaluation of 15+ LALMs reveals plausible and useful findings, e.g., Pure-to-Mixed degradation and universal weakness on Quality Assessment/Environment Reasoning subtasks.
weaknesses: Circularity / self-referential construction undermines the central claim that MECAT provides a reliable ground truth: all references are synthesized by a single LLM (DeepSeek-R1) from expert-model outputs, Audio Flamingo 2 is explicitly part of the annotation pipeline while Audio Flamingo 3 is an evaluated model, and the proposed DATE metric is validated primarily against an LLM-as-judge whose prompts were also authored by the same team. The benchmark risks measuring agreement with one LLM's stylistic conventions rather than human-level acoustic understanding.

The 'fine-grained' ground truth is itself machine-generated and demonstrably imperfect: only ~10% of candidates survive filtering, 85.3% of audited samples are merely 'acceptable or better,' and strict error is bounded at 3.4% -- yet model rankings with score gaps of 1-2 points (e.g., Table 2, Gemini-3-Pro 53.1 vs. Qwen3-Omni-Flash-1201 52.9) are presented as meaningful without a noise analysis linking annotation error to ranking uncertainty.

DATE's cross-sample discriminability component is dataset-relative: the score of a candidate depends on the composition of the entire test set (admitted in Sec. 6.4), which makes absolute scores non-comparable across subsets and complicates reporting; the metric's harmonic mean also couples two components with very different scales and interpretations. Only a single qualitative case study (Fig. 5A) and CDF separation against FENSE support superiority; correlation with human judgment rests on only 150 A/B pairs (means 90.9 vs. 49.3), with no per-pair statistics or correlation coefficient reported.

Several methodological details are unclear or appear erroneous: the GLAP filtering keeps a sample if similarity 'exceeds its average similarity ... by an empirically set threshold of 6' (a similarity exceeding an average by 6 is implausible; presumably 0.6 or a percentile?), the TF-IDF 'threshold of 6' phrasing is unexplained, and QA scoring is done by the same embedding-based DATE even though open-set QA answers were not shown to behave like captions.

Potential train/test contamination is not addressed: evaluated models (Qwen, Gemini, Baichuan, etc.) may have been pretrained on ACAV100M or on audio from the same YouTube sources, which could confound the reported model comparisons.

Presentation quality is below the venue's bar: grammatical errors throughout ('MECAT provide', 'penalizes semantically correct ... penalizes'), an empty 'Conflict of Interest Disclosure.' heading, multiple citation inconsistencies (Audio Flamingo 3 dated '2026', GLAP dated '2026', DeepSeek-R1 in Nature), and the metric is expanded as both 'Discriminative-Enhanced Audio Text Evaluation' (abstract) and 'Discriminability based Audio Task Evaluation' (Appendix E).

Reproducibility concerns: the GitHub link in the abstract is truncated/incomplete, and critical filtering thresholds, the discriminability reference-pool construction for QA, and the exact human-evaluator recruitment/compensation procedures are underspecified in the main text.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper convincingly identifies two real bottlenecks in current audio evaluation (coarse annotations and generic-caption-friendly metrics), and the related-work positioning (Table 1) clearly differentiates MECAT from AudioCaps, Clotho, MMAU, WavCaps-QA, etc., on test size, domain coverage, and data-source novelty (ACAV100M vs. the reused AudioSet/Clotho pool).

The multi-expert annotation pipeline (Figures 1, 3; Appendix C) is detailed and reproducible: content-specific (speech, music, sound) plus content-unrelated (quality, reverberation) expert models feed a CoT LLM synthesis stage with explicit synthesis rules and prompt templates provided in Appendices D and G.

Strong and multi-pronged validation of annotation quality: only ~10% of candidates survive GLAP/rule-based filtering, followed by a 150-pair human A/B test (>94% win rate over generic/incorrect captions; statistical parity with human references at 56.9%) and a 700-sample audit by 20 audio professionals with proper statistics (95% CI on the strict error rate, Wilcoxon tests with Bonferroni correction, effect sizes, per-category breakdown in Table F.3).

The DATE metric is well designed and empirically validated rather than merely asserted: qualitative case study (Figure 5-A), CDF discriminability analysis (Figure 5-B), bootstrap stability analysis with CV < 1% at full scale (Tables F.5/F.6), and human-alignment validation showing a large margin between human-preferred and non-preferred captions (90.9 vs. 49.3).

Comprehensive model evaluation: 17 captioning models and 15 QA models spanning caption-only models, audio-focused LALMs, omni LALMs, and proprietary systems, yielding genuinely useful findings (Pure-to-Mixed degradation of 10-25% on music/sound suggesting speech-centric bias; a capability dichotomy where Quality Assessment scores stay below 40 even for top models; hallucination in silent segments, Appendix L).

Good reproducibility practices: code and data publicly available, complete prompt templates, full model/prompt specifications (Appendix I), heuristic weights justified with a sensitivity analysis (Kendall's tau = 0.92 across alternative weightings, Table F.4), and an honest limitations section covering audio scope, residual annotation noise, and DATE's embedding-level blind spots (e.g., entity swaps, homogeneous corpora).
weaknesses: Circularity concerns in benchmark construction and evaluation: Audio Flamingo 2 is an explicit component of the annotation pipeline while Audio Flamingo 3 (its successor) is a system under evaluation, and Gemini models serve as the LLM-as-judge reference metric while Gemini systems are evaluated on the benchmark. Although the daggers and mid-pack AF3 scores suggest no overt favoritism, the paper would be stronger with an analysis quantifying potential advantage for models from the same family as pipeline components.

Baseline coverage for the DATE metric is thin: the central metric validation is against FENSE and BLEU-1 plus LLM-as-judge, with no comparison to other strong embedding-based metrics (e.g., BERTScore, MoverScore, SIGMA, or CLAP-based audio-text similarity scores). Claims of DATE's superiority over the family of semantic metrics are thus not fully substantiated.

DATE's cross-sample discriminability component is inherently dataset-dependent (rank of the matched reference within the full candidate pool), making it a benchmark-specific score rather than a general-purpose metric; this is partially acknowledged in the limitations but deserves more analysis of how the score behaves when reference quality or pool diversity varies.

Human validation is modest in scale for the central claims: the A/B test (N=150) that underpins both the annotation-quality claim and the DATE-human alignment claim is small, and the alignment result reports only mean scores (90.9 vs. 49.3) without a correlation coefficient, significance test, or per-pair analysis.

QA annotation quality appears less rigorously validated than captions: the REL audit and A/B test focus on captions, while the 100,000+ QA answers are LLM-generated from expert outputs and inherit upstream errors; no comparable direct human audit of QA correctness is reported.

Several construction details are under-specified or appear erroneous: the GLAP filtering 'threshold of 6' for a cosine-similarity criterion is not interpretable as written, and the pipeline's use of video title/description metadata raises a potential leakage concern (metadata-consistent but inaudible details) that is only indirectly mitigated by prompt rules.

Minor presentation issues: an empty 'Conflict of Interest Disclosure' heading on page 2, typos in Table C.1 ('Analsysis', 'Recogintion', 'Seperation'), and inconsistent model naming between main text and appendices (e.g., '-Instruct' suffixes appear only in Appendix tables) slightly reduce polish.
